Q: this my code for solving the following exercise about python lists: write a code to verify two list are circularly identical A:

You know that python supports list slicing (list[a:b] for gives all elements from a up to b-1), combining lists with + and comparing lists with ==. If you use those elements instead of handling a list element by element, the solution is actually as short and simple as any(l1 == l2[i:]+l2[:i] for i in range(len(l2)))

Q: Nominatim-responses from OpenStreetMap no longer readable A:

Use a custom User-Agent, not a browser/default one:

Response response = Jsoup
    .connect(url)
    .timeout(20000)
    .header("Accept-Encoding", "gzip,deflate,br")
    .userAgent("MyApp/1.0 (myemail@example.com)")
    .method(Method.GET)
    .maxBodySize(0)
    .ignoreContentType(true)
    .execute();

Nominatim’s usage policy requires identifiable clients; that’s why they block default browser UAs, and empty/generic UAs

Q: Why there are empty spaces in the middle of the string returned by re.split()? A:

Note the original Question you reference is about str.split(), not re.split() - while the usage is often similar, I highly doubt there's any designed intention to complement str.join() too and there's also no re.join()!

As for why, this is actually described in the re.split() docs

If there are capturing groups in the separator and it matches at the start of the string, the result will start with an empty string. The same holds for the end of the string

>>> re.split(r"(\s)", "Hello! How are you?")
['Hello!', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"\s", "Hello! How are you?")
['Hello!', 'How', 'are', 'you?']

Combined with @STerliakov's comment, we have a good explanation: using a capture group which matches a block will begin an empty string, then matching again leads to keeping this empty string

This Answer to How to group a regular expression in re.split() function? provides further insight, you can use a non-capturing group to skip these values in the results too

With a simpler string

>>> re.split(r"[12]", "0123")      # split on match, hole for successive
['0', '', '3']
>>> re.split(r"([12])", "0123")    # capture group keeps matches in result
['0', '1', '', '2', '3']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[12])", "0123")  # non-capturing group maintains hole
['0', '', '3']

So N matches leads to N-1 holes

>>> re.split(r"(?:[123])", "01234")
['0', '', '', '4']
>>> re.split(r"([123])", "01234")
['0', '1', '', '2', '', '3', '4']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789])", "0123456789")
['0', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '']

Combined with the quick duplicate marking (which suggests + to combine the successive matches), we can make make something a little nicer, with some choices dependent on if you want that ! and/or ? in the same result tokens

>>> re.split(r"(?:[12345678])", "0123456789")
['0', '', '', '', '', '', '', '', '9']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[12345678])+", "0123456789")
['0', '9']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789])+", "0123456789")  # unfortunately has trailing
['0', '']
>>> re.split(r"(?:[123456789]+)", "0123456789")  # when ending matches too
['0', '']

>>> re.split(r"(!|\s)", "Hello! How are you?")     # switch to OR
['Hello', '!', '', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"(!|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")    # OR with +
['Hello', ' ', 'How', ' ', 'are', ' ', 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"((!)|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")  # another capture group
['Hello', ' ', '!', 'How', ' ', None, 'are', ' ', None, 'you?']
>>> re.split(r"(?:(!)|\s)+", "Hello! How are you?")  # non-capture outer
['Hello', '!', 'How', None, 'are', None, 'you?']

Finally, you can always use filter(None, my_iterable) to drop Falsey values from some iterable and may also find re.findall() or re.finditer() is a better fit, though this steps around the explanation

>>> re.findall(r"\w+", "Hello! How are you?")       # "words"
['Hello', 'How', 'are', 'you']
>>> re.findall(r"[\w\?!]+", "Hello! How are you?")  # words and also ?,!
['Hello!', 'How', 'are', 'you?']
>>> re.findall(r"\w+|\?", "Hello! How are you?")    # ? is its own token
['Hello', 'How', 'are', 'you', '?']

Q: I found two solutions on how to generate points on a circle, within two radius values. One solutions favors the center, one does not. Why is this so? A:

"Naturally if we have points along these lines, then the points will seem to have more space between them, since angles "grow" as we get further from the origin" - this is exactly what happens.

The code generates a range of random points in a linear interval (a line, as you noted). But the density of points is only the same on each line:

The arc length from two consecutive points of angles a1 and a2 (a2 > a1) in a circle of radius r is given by:

C = 2 x PI x r x (a2 - a1)/360

(when a2=360 and a1=0 we get the circumference of the circle).

That increases as r increase.

As we go further from the origin, the density of points in the circumference decreases, since the number of points is the same, but the distance between them increases.

To mitigate this, one will need to repeat the distribution r/minRadius times for each value of r.

The points generated by the second code have the same density in all directions, since it have the same number of points in each line parallel to x axis and in each line parallel to y axis. In fact it generates a rectangle before the condition "Select points (x, y) that are > minRadius and < maxRadius". This condition only "cuts" the circle from the square.

Q: How to use an HTML # anchor in a dynamic URL A:

Your calling of an anchor within a dynamic URL is correct (Mozilla 2026). According to The Internet Society (2005) the syntax is:

[page]?[query]#[fragment]

Example: Open the "Egypt" Wikipedia page at the "Geography" heading.

Solution:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki?title=Egypt#Geography

What is happening?

  1. The query, not including the fragment, is sent to the server, resulting in the "Egypt" page being sent back to the client for rendering.
  2. The client browser now processes the fragment by finding the tag with the id attribute having the value Geography and scrolls down to it. (IBM 2026)

You will notice that the page source from Wikipedia (2026) contains the anchor element:
<h2 id="Geography">Geography</h2>

Why your code does not work?
The snippet of code you have shown is correct and the problem is likely not due to this. Without any error codes, screenshots or the full page.php source code, it will be almost impossible to deduce the cause. However, the statement about the duplicate content may be a clue:

I am redirected to page.php which has its content repeated vertically.

References
IBM (2026), The components of a URL, updated 16 January 2026, https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/cics-ts/6.x?topic=concepts-components-url

Mozilla (2026), URI Fragment, updated 02 March 2026, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/URI/Reference/Fragment

The Internet Society (2005), URI Generic Syntax, Request for Comments: 3986, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html#section-3.5

Wikipedia (2026), Egypt, updated 18 April 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt
